title: Work
subtitle: job or work, trades and professions, get the sack
summary: Name the people who work in a company, tell a trade from a profession, and use the everyday expressions people use about their working lives.

lesson.heading: Jobs in a workplace
rows: a member of the board of a company
an important person who makes big decisions
the person who runs the office day-to-day
makes sure the other workers are doing their job properly
trained to do specific tasks, e.g. building a computer
does a job that needs no training, e.g. an office cleaner
the person visitors must check in with
gives information about the company to the media
looks after the staff's interests in disputes with management

lesson.heading: job and work

left.label: job = a particular role or position
left.text: A **job** is countable. It is the post you hold, the one you apply for and the one you can lose.
examples: Jack's got a new **job** as a researcher.
Wish me luck in my new **job**.
A **job** in a museum wouldn't be as tiring as one in a restaurant.

right.label: work = the activities you do
right.text: **Work** is uncountable. It is what you actually do, and also the place where you do it.
examples: The best way of getting to **work** depends on where you live.
I'll pay for the plumbing **work** when it's finished.

lesson.note: Say the way to work, not ~~the way to job~~, and my new job, not ~~my new work~~.

lesson.heading: Trades and professions
rows: takes the decisions in legal cases
works for a government department, putting policies into action
the chief diplomat representing his or her government abroad
treats muscle injury by rubbing and moving the injured area
plans how something will look and work
skilled at making things with wood
works with the supply and connection of water pipes
puts out fires and rescues people
looks after other people's children in her own home while the parents are at work
lesson.note: **Professions** need considerable training and/or qualifications. **Trades** are skilled manual jobs that need on-the-job training.

lesson.heading: Collocations: talking about work
lesson.text: These are the phrases people actually use when they talk about earning money. Notice **make a living** (earn enough money to live comfortably) and **take on** a job, which suggests accepting personal responsibility for it.

examples.text: It's not easy to **get work** round these parts.
*A:* What do you **do for a living**? *B:* I'm **in** publishing.
It's hard to **make a living** as a freelance writer.
She's not prepared to **take on** that job.

lesson.heading: Hours of work
lesson.text: If you **do shiftwork** (or **work shifts**), your hours change: nights one week, days the next. **Flexi-time** lets you choose your hours, and **nine-to-five** is ordinary regular day work.

examples.text: One week it's six-to-two, the next it's nights - he **does shiftwork**.
examples.note: also: he works shifts / he's a shiftworker

examples.text: I'm **on flexi-time**, so I can start at seven if I want to.
I get in at nine and go home at five - I **work nine-to-five**.

lesson.heading: Leaving a job - and time off
lesson.text: There are polite words and blunt words for losing a job. **Get the sack** and **be laid off** are informal; **be fired** and **be made redundant** are more formal. If you are **made redundant**, the company no longer needs the job, so it is nobody's fault.

examples.text: I was late so often that I **got the sack**.
examples.note: more formal: I was fired / I was dismissed

examples.text: Two hundred workers were **made redundant** when the plant closed.
The drivers have decided to **go on strike**.
He's only 58, but he's taken **early retirement**.
I'm not working now; the baby's due in three weeks, so I'm on **maternity leave**.
examples.note: for a father it is paternity leave

examples.text: She's been off on **sick leave** since January.

lesson.heading: Getting on at work
lesson.text: To **apply for** a job you fill in forms and send them off. If you are **promoted**, you are given a higher position. A **workaholic** loves work far too much.

examples.text: I'd love to **apply for** a job in journalism, but it's not easy without qualifications.
They've made her General Manager, so she's been **promoted**.
Your trouble is you're obsessed with work - you're a **workaholic**.

lesson.text: Remember the pair: you *apply for* a job but you *do* work. If a word like *some* or *much* fits in front of it, the word you want is *work*.

exercises.prompt: Match each job title with the description that fits it.

pairs.right: represents the workers in disputes with management
has a high position and makes important decisions
sits on the board of the company
does a job that needs no special training
runs the day-to-day organisation of a department
keeps an eye on the daily work of other workers

exercises.prompt: I'll pay for the plumbing ___ when it's finished.
exercises.explanation: Work is the activity that is done; it is uncountable here.

exercises.prompt: I'd like to apply for a ___ in your office.
exercises.explanation: A job is one particular position, so it takes a.

exercises.prompt: Is each of these a trade or a profession?
'I'm not working now; the baby's due in three weeks.' She's on ___.
exercises.explanation: Maternity leave is the time a mother takes off before and after the birth.

exercises.prompt: 'He's enjoying life on a pension, although he's only 58.' He's taken ___.
exercises.explanation: Take early retirement = stop working before the normal age.

exercises.prompt: 'They've made her General Manager as from next month!' She's been ___.
exercises.explanation: Be promoted = be given a higher position.

exercises.prompt: 'I was late so often that I lost my job.' I got ___.
exercises.explanation: Get the sack is the informal way of saying you were dismissed.

exercises.prompt: Since I have to earn a ___ somehow, I'll take whatever work I can find.
exercises.explanation: Earn / make a living = earn enough money to live on.

exercises.prompt: I've been offered some part-time work editing a book, but I'm not sure I want to ___.
exercises.explanation: Take on a job = accept it and the responsibility that comes with it.

exercises.prompt: Ask someone what their job is. The answer is: 'I'm in banking.'
exercises.answer: What do you do for a living?
exercises.explanation: What do you do for a living? is the natural way to ask about someone's job.

exercises.statement: If you are made redundant, the company no longer needs your job.
exercises.explanation: Correct. Being made redundant means the post itself has gone. Laid off is the informal version.

exercises.statement: Someone who works nine-to-five does shiftwork.
exercises.explanation: Nine-to-five is regular day work. Shiftwork means your hours change - nights one week, days the next.
